description: 5 HARD-level code questions on Python Variables (Part 1 of 2). Dynamic typing, multiple assignment/unpacking, chained assignment, starred unpacking, and augmented assignment evaluation order. Computed outputs verified with Python 3.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

x = 42
x = "forty-two"
print(x)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
forty-two

EXPLANATION:
Python is dynamically typed: a variable is just a name bound to an object. Reassigning x from an integer to a string is perfectly legal - Python never locks a name to a single type. The last assignment wins, so print(x) shows "forty-two".

code:
x = 42          # x -> int 42
x = "forty-two" # x -> str "forty-two" (rebinding is allowed)
print(x)        # forty-two

WHY IT MATTERS:
A C/Java developer can't imagine this, but it is exactly why Python lets you write defs that return different types. The trade-off: type errors surface at runtime, not compile time. The old int object (42) becomes garbage once no name references it.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
a, b = b, c
print(a, b, c)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
2 3 3

EXPLANATION:
The right-hand side of an assignment is fully evaluated BEFORE any name is written. On the second line, b and c are read first (2 and 3), and only then are those values assigned - a becomes 2, b becomes 3. c is untouched and stays 3.

code:
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3   # a=1, b=2, c=3
a, b = b, c         # read (2, 3) first, then a=2, b=3
print(a, b, c)      # 2 3 3

WHY IT MATTERS:
The "read RHS before writing" rule is what makes Python swaps, rotating values, and parallel iteration (for k, v in d.items()) safe and concise. Getting this wrong means expecting a=3 here (b was 2 when read - not a=... whatever you mutated). RHS is always the OLD state.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

a = b = 5
b = 10
print(a, b)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
5 10

EXPLANATION:
a = b = 5 binds both names to the same integer object 5. Integers are IMMUTABLE, so b = 10 does not modify that object - it rebinds only b to a brand-new int object 10. a still refers to the original 5.

code:
a = b = 5   # both a and b point at the int object 5
b = 10      # b now points at a new object; a is untouched
print(a, b) # 5 10

WHY IT MATTERS:
This same pattern is a famous TRAP with mutable objects:
x = y = []
x.append(1)
print(y)   # [1] - x and y share the SAME list object!
For immutables (int, str, tuple) chained assignment is harmless; for mutables (list, dict, set) it creates shared references. Use x = []; y = [] to create independent lists.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

first, *rest = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(first, rest)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
10 [20, 30, 40]

EXPLANATION:
In a starred assignment, the *rest target collects ALL leftover items into a list. first gets the first element (10), rest gets everything after it as a list [20, 30, 40].

code:
first, *rest = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(first, rest)  # 10 [20, 30, 40]

# Edge cases:
first, *rest = [1]     # rest -> [] (empty list, no error)
first, *rest = []      # ValueError: not enough values to unpack

WHY IT MATTERS:
Starred unpacking handles a variable-length head/tail without slicing:
head, *body, tail = rows     # first row, all middle rows, last row
name, *tags, domain = email.split("@")  # flexible splits
The star can appear exactly once per pattern but in any position (first, middle, or last).

questions.question:
What does this code print?

x = 6
x *= 3 + 1
print(x)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
24

EXPLANATION:
x *= 3 + 1 is shorthand for x = x * (3 + 1). The right-hand side is evaluated FIRST (3 + 1 = 4), then the multiplication happens: 6 * 4 = 24. The common wrong guess is 19 (6 * 3 + 1), which ignores the parentheses' precedence.

code:
x = 6
x *= 3 + 1        # x = x * (3 + 1) -> 6 * 4
print(x)          # 24

WHY IT MATTERS:
Augmented assignment evaluates the ENTIRE right side before combining. The same rule applies to lists with += (which also mutates in place via __iadd__) and to all operators: +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=, &=, |=. Parenthesize the operand when in doubt.
